extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, students and scholars of poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing tragedy (dramatic/epic plot, characters, thought, diction, musical and visual ornament) based on Aristotle's Art of Poetry with commentary and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as imitation of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the Imitation of an Action; and consequently, is chiefly an Imitation of those who Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The art of tragedy is fundamentally the representation of a complete action; the poet must imitate agents and their deeds rather than merely describe states. Because actions cannot occur without characters (manners), the imitation of action entails attention to agents and their moral/psychological dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject/Plot (fable) is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: That Subject has the first place in Tragedy (the Subject is in that Poem what the Sketches are in Painting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot (subject/fable) is the foremost element: a poet should first arrange the strokes of the action (the structure of events) before adding characters or ornament. A well-ordered plot produces the principal pleasure of tragedy; a confused plot cannot be redeemed by other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners/Character are second in importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manners follow next...Manners are always the Cause of Actions; therefore after the Subject, Manners are the next most important in Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters (manners) must be properly disposed so that, when seen in a testing situation, the audience can foresee what side they will take and how they will behave. Good characters enable the spectator to judge likely outcomes of incidents. Anti-pattern: 'huddling' manners or failing to give characters stable dispositions leads to uncertainty and weakens the tragedy's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments/Thought are third
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Manners, come the Sentiments; that is to say, the Faculty of expressing those things which belong to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought (sentences, moral remarks, arguments) must express what belongs to the subject. Sentiments should follow truth where necessary and verisimilitude where probability is at issue. There are two ways to find appropriate sentiments: policy (what is naturally found in the subject) and rhetoric (artful embellishment). Rhetorical embellishment requires study; misuse can betray truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction/Elocution is less essential (fourth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth thing...is the Diction. Of all the essential Parts of Tragedy, Diction is of the least importance, though it extremely enhances the Beauty of a Piece when it is Noble and proportioned to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good diction refines and clarifies thought but a tragedy can be perfect in its effects even if elocution is faulty. Poor elocution flattens discourse but does not necessarily destroy the merits of plot, character, or thought. Diction has equal force in prose and verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse vs Prose for diction (harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse is only used, because that Diction is more harmonious, and consequently more agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While diction functions in both prose and verse, verse is chosen for its greater harmony and agreeable effect; this is an ornamental enhancement rather than an essential structural requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as chief ornament (fifth)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Diction, comes the Music, which is the most agreeable of all that Tragedy can employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music is an added seasoning that refines the passions and greatly pleases audiences; it is preferable even to dancing or decor. Historically, composers arranged different kinds of music for different audiences (soft/sweet vs. loud/brisk) to please a wider public. Music is not strictly necessary to the poet's art but is the most powerful agreeable adjunct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration/Spectacle is external ornament (last)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Decoration...comprehends all that makes the Beauty of the Shows as the Scene, the Ornaments, the Machines, the Habits of the Actors...The Decoration is more the Business of Engineers and Workmen than the Poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenic decoration and machinery delight the eye and elevate the show but do not constitute the poet's art. The poet should nonetheless be able to judge what is proper or improper for his pieces. Excessive focus on decoration (or treating it as poetry) mistakes the workmanship of engineers for poetic creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude (probable truth) must be followed
rubrics_metrics.description: At least Verisimilitude must be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exact truth cannot be observed, what is said must at least be probable and consistent with the subject. Example: a poet may represent a madman speaking either exactly as a madman would or as a probable version of such speech; failing either truth or verisimilitude breaks audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and method in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Poet...doth not huddle his Manners...but begins by disposing the Plot and all the Parts of the Action; and afterwards adds those Manners which are proper to render the Action credible and probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a natural order: outline the plot (action) first, assign characters and their dispositions afterwards, then craft sentiments, diction, music, and decoration. Anti-pattern: hasty composition that mixes elements without order (analogy: a painter mixing colours confusedly) produces less pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be entire: beginning, middle, end
rubrics_metrics.description: I call that Entire, which hath a Beginning, a Middle, and an End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action suitable for tragedy or epic must have these three parts: a beginning (which supposes nothing necessary before it and requires something after), a middle (which presupposes something before and requires something after), and an end (which requires nothing after it). These definitions prohibit giving a 'beginning to the beginning' or adding unnecessary sequels after the proper end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just extent/magnitude of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the Imitation of an Action that is perfect and entire, and of a Just extent...Beauty consists in order and in the Magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action's magnitude must be such that spectators can apprehend it at once or retain it in memory: not so small that it is merely momentaneous (and thus inappropriate as a full plot), and not so large that it becomes incoherent or exceeds the audience's capacity for comprehension. The precise duration cannot be fixed by rule but must suit the nature of the poem and the verisimilitude of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous episodes; middle must relate to whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The Middle is that which supposes something which ought to precede it, and requires something which ought to follow...that which suppose nothing before them nor require nothing after them, are no part of an Action; They are foreign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all parts of the middle are causally related to the beginning and end. Avoid independent incidents or digressions that do not contribute to the main action (anti-pattern exemplified by Statius giving unrelated sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet must master related arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Though properly speaking the Fable regards the Poet, the Manners depend on Morality, the Sentiments on Rhetorick, and the Diction on Grammar; nevertheless a Poet ought to be instructed in all those Arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should be knowledgeable in morality, rhetoric, grammar, music, and practical judgement about spectacle; mastery of these allied disciplines is necessary because poetry presupposes and integrates them, even if some are technically separate arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy vs Rhetoric for finding suitable sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy is for those things which are naturally found in the Subject...Rhetorick is for these things which are agreeable to the Subject, and embellish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'policy' (general considerations, common usage) to derive what naturally belongs to the subject; use rhetoric when you need to embellish or produce agreeable but artful discourse. Rhetorical devices require art and careful study to avoid mistaking artifice for truth; corrupted speakers use rhetoric only to pursue ends rather than truth.
